```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(width = 100)
```

sciparseR reads scientific articles, PDF or JATS XML, and returns two
things: a **document model** that describes what is on each page and where,
and an **extraction** that lists the scientific facts found in the document
together with the exact text that supports each of them. This article walks
through the whole workflow on a small synthetic trial report that ships
with the package.

```{r}
library(sciparseR)
pdf <- system.file("extdata", "trial_tables.pdf", package = "sciparseR")
```

## 1. Parse

`sc_parse()` detects the format from the file content and runs the parser.
No network access and no external program is needed.

```{r}
doc <- sc_parse(pdf)
doc
```

The printout already shows the provenance that every later step relies
on: a document identifier derived from the SHA-256 checksum of the file,
the parser backend and versions, and the schema version of the model.

```{r}
str(doc$processing[c("package_version", "r_version", "config_hash")])
doc$processing$backend
```

## 2. Look at the structure

The document is a list of tidy data frames. Blocks are paragraphs,
headings, captions, tables and so on, in reading order:

```{r}
b <- sc_blocks(doc)
b[, c("block_id", "page", "type", "reading_order")]
```

Sections form a tree with canonical labels such as `methods` and
`results`, which the extraction layer uses to decide where to look:

```{r}
sc_sections(doc)[, c("section_id", "level", "title", "label")]
```

The text can be reconstructed in reading order, without running headers
and page numbers:

```{r}
cat(substr(sc_text(doc), 1, 600))
```

## 3. Tables

Tables keep their cell structure: spans, header rows, footnote markers and
missing value markers. Data frames are a view on top of the cells.

```{r}
sc_tables(doc)[, c("table_id", "label", "n_rows", "n_cols", "n_header_rows", "ruled")]
sc_table_to_dataframe(doc, "Table 2")
```

## 4. Extract

The rules engine is deterministic: same document, same configuration, same
result.

```{r}
x <- sc_extract(doc, "clinical_trial")
x
```

Study level facts are plain records:

```{r}
r <- x$records
r[is.na(r$observation_id) & r$status == "reported", c("field", "value", "arm")]
```

Numerical results are grouped into observations. Each number keeps the
context it was bound to and where that binding came from:

```{r}
w <- sc_observations(x, wide = TRUE)
w[w$field == "result", c("outcome", "arm", "comparator", "timepoint", "analysis_set",
                         "effect_measure", "estimate", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_value")]
```

## 5. Evidence

Every value points to its evidence: page, section, block or table cell,
the exact source text, character offsets and a bounding box.

```{r}
ev <- sc_evidence(x)
ev[ev$field == "randomized_n", c("value", "page", "section_label", "char_start", "char_end", "bbox_scope")]
with(ev[ev$field == "randomized_n", ][1, ], substring(text, char_start, char_end))
```

## 6. Validate and review

```{r}
x <- sc_validate(x)
table(x$validation$rule, x$validation$result)
sc_review_queue(x)[, c("priority", "field", "statistic", "value", "reason")]
```

The review queue lists what a person should look at: here an estimate in
a sentence that does not name its outcome, a plus-minus value whose type
(SD or SE) the authors never stated, and cells that are empty or marked
missing in the source. sciparseR never fills these gaps on its own.

## 7. Export

```{r}
out <- tempfile(fileext = ".json")
sc_export_json(x, out)
y <- sc_read_json(out)
identical(y$records, x$records)
```
